title: Nitrogen cycle
group: BIO-EVOL / BIO-ECOL / BIO-PLANT — Evolution, Ecology & Plants
examples: How do bacteria help with the nitrogen cycle?
What is the role of nitrogen fixation in the environment?
Can you explain the difference between nitrification and denitrification?

explain.say: Today we will learn about the nitrogen cycle. This cycle moves nitrogen between different parts of nature.
First is nitrogen fixation. Certain bacteria can take atmospheric nitrogen gas. They convert this gas into usable compounds for plants.
Next is nitrification. This is a two-step process done by different bacteria. They change ammonia into nitrates which plants love to use.
The third stage is denitrification. Here, different bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas. This completes the cycle by returning gas to the air.
In everyday life, this cycle is important for soil health. When plants die, bacteria break down the nitrogen, making it available again for new growth.

draw.text: Soil health depends on N cycling

explain.say: A common mistake is thinking all bacteria perform all steps. Remember that different groups of bacteria handle specific parts of the cycle.

faq.q: Why is the nitrogen cycle important for life on Earth?
faq.a: Nitrogen is a vital component of proteins and DNA. The cycle ensures that nitrogen is constantly recycled and available for all living things.
asks: What happens if nitrogen runs out?
Is nitrogen needed for building life?

faq.q: Which bacteria are responsible for nitrogen fixation?
faq.a: Some types of bacteria, like those found in root nodules, have the enzyme nitrogenase. This allows them to break the strong triple bond in N₂ gas.
asks: What enzyme do bacteria use for this?

faq.q: What is the difference between nitrification and denitrification?
faq.a: Nitrification converts ammonia to usable nitrates, which plants absorb. Denitrification reverses this, turning nitrates back into atmospheric nitrogen gas.
asks: What happens to nitrates in the soil?
Which process releases nitrogen to the air?

faq.q: Does the nitrogen cycle happen only in soil?
faq.a: No, this cycle occurs in many environments. It happens in water bodies, the atmosphere, and within living organisms as well.
asks: Can this happen in the ocean?
Is it only a soil process?

faq.q: What is the role of atmospheric nitrogen?
faq.a: Atmospheric nitrogen, N₂, is abundant but usually too stable to be used directly by plants. Bacteria are needed to make it usable.
asks: Why can't plants use N₂ gas directly?

facts: Atmospheric nitrogen is mostly present as N₂ gas.
Nitrogen fixation converts N₂ into ammonia or ammonium.
Nitrification converts ammonia to nitrite, then to nitrate.
Denitrification returns nitrogen gas to the atmosphere.

quiz.say: If a plant is struggling to grow, which process might be deficient in the soil?
quiz.show: Which process is needed for plant growth?
quiz.why: Nitrification creates nitrates (NO₃⁻), which are the form most easily absorbed by plant roots.

wrong.0: Denitrification removes usable nitrogen from the soil, which would cause deficiency.
wrong.1: Decomposition is the breakdown of matter, but nitrification is the specific step creating absorbable nitrates.
wrong.3: Fixation is important, but it converts gas to ammonia, which is not the primary form plants absorb.

quiz.say: Bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds through which process?
quiz.why: Nitrogen fixation is the specific term for converting inert atmospheric nitrogen gas into reactive forms like ammonia.

wrong.0: Denitrification is the process of losing nitrogen gas back to the atmosphere.
wrong.1: Ammonification is the breakdown of organic matter, not the initial conversion of N₂ gas.
wrong.3: Nitrification happens after fixation, changing ammonia to nitrates.

quiz.say: What is the final product released back into the atmosphere during the cycle?
quiz.why: Denitrification is the final step that converts nitrates back into the inert N₂ gas found in the atmosphere.

wrong.0: Nitrate is a usable form that remains in the soil, not the final gas released.
wrong.1: Nitrite is an intermediate product that is quickly converted to nitrate.
wrong.3: Ammonia is an intermediate product, usually formed during fixation or decomposition.
